per_claim.claim_text: The UK Strategic Road Network carries approximately one-third of all road traffic and two-thirds of freight tonne-kilometres , yet its adaptive capacity to changing climate conditions is under strain.
per_claim.source_quote: We must consider how the changing climate will affect our strategic road network - the 4,500 miles of motorways and major A-roads we manage including bridges, tunnels, drains and earthworks.
per_claim.reasoning: The PDF confirms the SRN exists and faces climate pressure, but contains no traffic-share figures (one-third) or freight tonne-kilometre statistics — those quantitative claims are not supported by this document.

per_claim.claim_text: The UK Department for Transport's Rapid Evidence Assessment identifies a need for better understanding of climate change impacts on road infrastructure and highlights that cost-benefit analyses of adaptation remain limited and methodologically challenging .
per_claim.reasoning: The PDF makes no reference to the Department for Transport, a Rapid Evidence Assessment, cost-benefit analysis, or any methodological discussion; the source is a short National Highways web page covering their own adaptation strategy, not a DfT review.

per_claim.claim_text: The map translates per-millimetre coefficients into absolute scenario impacts that are directly interpretable by transport planners and drainage engineers.} Beyond targeting, the near-zero sensitivity of the most resilient corridors (A11, A1(M)) implies that higher design standards, particularly the drainage capacity specified in the DMRB for motorways and high-speed dual carriageways, may themselves constitute an effective form of climate resilience, a finding relevant to debates about investment standards for new construction .
per_claim.reasoning: This claim contains bespoke empirical findings (per-mm coefficients, A11/A1(M) corridor sensitivity, DMRB drainage standards) that are entirely absent from this four-page web document; the claim appears to be original analysis from the citing paper itself, not content attributable to this source.
